title: Comcast Beats Q2 Estimates as Peacock Turns First Profit Ahead of NBCUniversal Spinoff
excerpt: The cable giant's streaming service posted $189 million in pre-tax income while the company beat earnings and revenue estimates, bolstering the case for its planned media business separation.
body:
Comcast beat Wall Street's second-quarter estimates on Thursday, reporting adjusted earnings of $1.04 per share on revenue of $29.94 billion — surpassing analyst expectations of $0.97 and $29.24 billion, respectively, according to FactSet. Shares climbed 3.3% in premarket trading to $24.29.

The standout was Peacock. The streaming service, launched in 2020 and long a drag on the company's bottom line, posted its first-ever quarterly profit — $189 million in pre-tax income — driven by the FIFA World Cup and a strong summer content slate. Revenue surged 54% year-over-year to $1.9 billion.

Peacock Takes Flight

Peacock added 2 million paid subscribers during the quarter, nearly four times what analysts polled by Visible Alpha had expected, bringing its total to 48 million. The growth was powered by Telemundo's Spanish-language FIFA World Cup coverage, which benefited from prime-time kickoffs in the U.S., along with the hit reality show "Love Island USA."

"Peacock reached profitability for the first time, supported by a broad slate of sports, entertainment and major live events that drove strong engagement across our platforms."

— Brian L. Roberts and Mike Cavanagh, Co-CEOs of Comcast

The milestone is significant for a streaming service that spent billions to carve out a foothold against Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon Prime Video. It also strengthens the business case for Comcast's planned spinoff of NBCUniversal and Sky, announced June 29.

Studios and Media Deliver

Media revenue climbed 25% to $5.69 billion, with about $441 million attributed to World Cup gains. The studio division posted 25% revenue growth to $3 billion, buoyed by unexpected box-office hit "Obsession" and the animated "The Super Mario Galaxy Movie." The strong entertainment performance came weeks after "The Odyssey" opened to blockbuster numbers, further validating NBCUniversal's content strategy.

Broadband Bleeding Slows — But Doesn't Stop

Comcast lost 167,000 domestic broadband customers during the quarter, slightly above the 165,000 analysts had predicted. That is still an improvement from the 201,000 lost in the same period a year earlier, but underscores persistent competitive pressure from T-Mobile, Verizon's fixed-wireless offerings and fiber rivals aggressively expanding their networks. Broadband service revenue fell 5.5% to $6.28 billion.

Video customer losses narrowed to 280,000 from 325,000 a year ago. The one bright spot in connectivity: wireless. Comcast added 448,000 domestic wireless lines — well above the 379,000 expected — and surpassed 10 million total lines for the first time. With penetration below 7% of addressable lines, according to the company, there is substantial room to grow.

Spinoff Comes Into Focus

These results are the first since Comcast announced plans to split into two publicly traded companies. The new NBCUniversal entity, to be led by co-CEO Mike Cavanagh, will house Universal theme parks, film and TV studios, NBC, Peacock and European media business Sky. Michael Angelakis, a former CFO, will return as CEO of the standalone connectivity company.

The stock has lost nearly 30% over the past year, making it one of the cheapest in the S&P 500. Benchmark Equity Research analyst Matthew Harrigan has assigned a $44 price target, implying more than 80% upside. The spinoff is expected to complete in roughly a year.

Theme parks were the quarter's soft spot. Adjusted EBITDA for the parks unit fell 5.1%, with revenue of $2.41 billion slightly missing estimates.

What to Watch

Comcast generated $4.6 billion in free cash flow and returned $2.1 billion to shareholders during the quarter. Overall profit fell to $3.53 billion, or 99 cents per share, from $11.12 billion a year earlier — a figure inflated by one-time items.

The dual narrative — a thriving media business about to be set free and a connectivity arm fighting to stabilize — will define the next 12 months as the company executes the most consequential corporate restructuring in its history.
